questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to apply simple bit-tricks succinctly and reason about edge cases without loops. It also shows understanding of bitwise adjacency relationships across 64 bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise AND and right shift
- Detecting pattern overlap without branching
- Constant-time evaluation on fixed width integers

## Code Example

```javascript
function hasConsecutiveOnes(n) {
  // n treated as a 64-bit value; bitwise ops apply to 32-bit in JS
  return (n & (n >>> 1)) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend to count how many adjacent pairs exist?
- How would you test correctness with edge inputs like all zeros, all ones, alternating patterns?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests precise bit-twiddling without branches; validates wraparound understanding and constant-time composition.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation (circular shift)
- Modulo reduction via masking (k & 63)

uint64_t rotateLeft64(uint64_t x, unsigned int k) {

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests precise bit-level reasoning and avoids expensive operations in tight loops, useful in storage engines and query optimizers.

## Key Concepts

- Single-set-bit test: (n & (n-1)) == 0
- Even-index bit mask: 0x55555555
- Combining tests with boolean logic for a robust check

## Code Example

```javascript
function isSingleEvenBitSet(n) {
  return n !== 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0 && (n & 0x55555555) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you generalize to check exactly k bits set?
- How would you adapt to 64-bit width and different bit-ordering considerations?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests branchless bitwise selection across a 128-bit value. It mirrors practical use cases like compositing two 128-bit values with a mask in a single pass.

## Key Concepts

- Branchless bitwise selection
- 128-bit composition via hi/lo fields
- Handling of full-range masks across both lanes

## Code Example

```c
uint128 blend128(uint128 a, uint128 b, uint128 mask) {
  uint128 t1 = and128(a, mask);
  uint128 t2 = and128(b, not128(mask));
  return or128(t1, t2);
}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Matters
Tests the ability to implement bitwise rotation on 128-bit words without branches, while safely handling edge cases.

## Key Concepts
- **Bitwise rotation**: Moves bits cyclically; bits shifted out one end re-enter from the other.
- **Safe shift masking**: The `k &= 127` constrains k to [0, 127], preventing undefined behavior when k >= word width.
- **No loops or conditionals**: Shift and OR operations execute in constant time for low-latency systems.

## Code Breakdown
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 127;                    // mask to valid range
  return (x << k) | (x >> (128 - k));  // rotate via split-shift-OR
}
```
- `(x << k)` moves the high bits toward the left, discarding overflow.
- `(x >> (128 - k))` captures the bits that "wrap around" to the right.
- OR combines both halves into a single cyclic result.

## Why This Is Asked

Swapping adjacent nibble pairs is a compact test of masking and shifting, with deterministic result and no branching. It exercises understanding of nibble boundaries and how to apply masks to rearrange 4-bit chunks.

## Key Concepts

- Bit masks and shifts
- 32-bit nibble alignment
- Compositional bitwise operations

## Code Example

```javascript
uint32_t swapNibbles32(uint32_t x) {
  return ((x & 0x0F0F0F0F) << 4) | ((x & 0xF0F0F0F0) >> 4);
}
```
